Here's the reality from your schema and harvester:

What's stored on a contact today: company, website, industry, location, employee_count, email, phone, website_score, opportunity_score, icp_score, icp_tier, revenue_leak, intel_pills, size_signals, status, report_slug... and that's it. There's no dimensions column, no load time, no booking flag, no rating. The report's been reading c.dimensions, but the table never stores it — so on a real fetch, dimensions is empty and the report falls back to defaults. That explains why the breakdown has felt generic.

Where the good data actually lives: audit_url() in scraper/engine.py clearly computes a rich dimensions object (the harvester reads audit["dimensions"]["mobile"]["mobile_issues"]), plus audit["website_score"], mobile_issues, revenue_leak, etc. But the harvester's contact = {...} block doesn't persist dimensions — it throws that detail away and only saves the top-line scores. Claude responded: We can — but it costs you something, so let me lay out the tradeoff honestly rather than just saying yes.

We can — but it costs you something, so let me lay out the tradeoff honestly rather than just saying yes.

Why it's an estimate right now: fetch_page uses httpx — it fetches the raw HTML and times that single request. That's server response time, not real load time. It never downloads images, CSS, JS, or runs the page, which is why mobile is faked as desktop × 2.5. A roofer's site that responds in 0.8s but takes 9s to actually render would look fast to your current code.

To get the exact measurement, you need to actually render the page in a real browser engine, on a throttled mobile profile. Two routes:

Option A — Google PageSpeed Insights API (recommended). Google runs Lighthouse on their servers and hands you back the real numbers. You already pay nothing for it (free, ~25k calls/day with a key).

  • You get real measured mobile and desktop, separately — First Contentful Paint, Largest Contentful Paint, Time to Interactive, Speed Index, and the overall Performance score.
  • It's the same engine Google uses to rank you, so the number is credible and defensible to a prospect ("this is Google's own score for your site").
  • One extra HTTP call per site in the harvester. Adds ~3-6s per site to harvesting.
  • Downside: it's an external dependency and occasionally rate-limits on big batches.

Option B — Playwright (you already have it for screenshots). Since you're already launching a headless browser for the device mockups, you can read the real load timing from that same page load (performance.timing / navigation API) on a mobile viewport with network throttling. No extra service, reuses work you're already doing. Slightly less authoritative than "Google says," and throttling has to be configured to mean anything.

My recommendation: PageSpeed Insights. The number becomes measured and Google-branded, which is far more persuasive in a recommendations report than your own estimate — and it gives you real mobile vs. desktop split, which kills the ×2.5 fudge entirely.

The clean architecture: add a lighthouse.py helper that calls PSI, returns {mobile_lcp, desktop_lcp, mobile_perf, desktop_perf, ...}, store those on the contact, and the speed dimension + bullets read real values. Falls back to the current httpx estimate if PSI fails, so nothing breaks.

Claude responded: Both are doable, but they're not equally easy.

Both are doable, but they're not equally easy. Here's the honest comparison.

PageSpeed Insights — easier to implement, with a setup step.

The code is genuinely tiny — it's one HTTP call, which fits your existing httpx pattern perfectly:

python
async def measure_speed(url):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=60) as c:
        r = await c.get("https://www.googleapis.com/pagespeedonline/v5/runPagespeed",
            params={"url": url, "strategy": "mobile", "key": PSI_KEY})
    d = r.json()
    lcp = d["lighthouseResult"]["audits"]["largest-contentful-paint"]["numericValue"]/1000
    return round(lcp, 1)

That's basically it. No new dependencies, no browser, no infra. The "work" is non-code: get a free API key from Google Cloud Console (enable the PageSpeed Insights API, generate a key, drop it in your env vars next to SERPAPI_KEY). Five minutes, but it's a step.

The catches: each call takes 3-8 seconds (Google is rendering the whole page), and for mobile+desktop that's two calls per site. On a 28-site batch that's a few minutes added. And it occasionally rate-limits on large runs, so you'd want a fallback to your current estimate.

Playwright — no setup, but more code and more fragility.

No API key, no external service — you reuse the browser you're already launching for screenshots. But the code is more involved: you have to apply mobile device emulation, configure network throttling (without throttling the number is meaningless — a datacenter connection isn't a roofer's customer on 4G), wait for the right load event, then read performance.getEntriesByType('navigation'). Throttling in Playwright means dropping into the CDP session, which is fiddly. And the number is "your measurement" rather than "Google's score," so it's less persuasive to a prospect.

My honest take: PSI is the easier and better choice. The only friction is the one-time key setup, and in exchange you get a real, Google-branded, measured number for both mobile and desktop — which is exactly the credible per-site figure you wanted for the bullets. Playwright avoids the key but trades it for more brittle code and a weaker claim.

Claude responded: .

.gitignore is a plain text file that tells Git which files to ignore — meaning never track, never commit, never push to GitHub. Git reads it automatically; you don't run anything.

Why it matters right now: without it, the next time you run your PowerShell git commands (git add .), your .env.local file — with your PSI key, Supabase service key, and SerpAPI key inside it — would get committed and pushed to your public-ish GitHub repo. Anyone who sees the repo then has your keys. People get bots scraping GitHub for exactly this. So .gitignore is the thing standing between "secrets safe on my machine" and "secrets published to the internet."

How it works: it lives in your repo root (C:\Users\steve\prospect-engine\.gitignore), and each line is a filename or pattern to skip. For a Python project like yours it'd contain things like:

.env
.env.local
__pycache__/
*.pyc
venv/
.venv/

Any file matching a line there is invisible to Git.

Let's just check yours. In PowerShell, from your repo folder, run:

powershell
cat .gitignore

Three outcomes:

  • It prints a list and .env.local is in it → you're safe, nothing to do.
  • It prints a list but .env.local is missing → add it:
powershell
  Add-Content .gitignore "`n.env.local"
  • You get an error like "Cannot find path" → the file doesn't exist, so create it:
powershell
  Set-Content .gitignore ".env`n.env.local`n__pycache__/`n*.pyc`n.venv/"

One more safety check — make sure the key isn't already tracked from a past commit. Run:

powershell
git status

If you see .env.local listed under "Changes to be committed" or "Untracked files" that's the moment to fix it before your next git add. If it's already been committed in the past, tell me and I'll give you the steps to scrub it (it's a bit more involved — git rm --cached).

Paste what cat .gitignore and git status show and I'll confirm you're clean before we go near the code.

Here's the complete code. Create scraper/lighthouse.py in your repo and paste all of this in:

python
"""
PageSpeed Insights — real measured load time (mobile + desktop).
Falls back gracefully: if PSI fails or no key, returns {} and the
caller keeps using the httpx load_time estimate.
"""
import os
import asyncio
import httpx

PSI_KEY = os.environ.get("PSI_KEY", "")
PSI_URL = "https://www.googleapis.com/pagespeedonline/v5/runPagespeed"


async def _run(url: str, strategy: str) -> dict:
    params = {"url": url, "strategy": strategy, "category": "performance"}
    if PSI_KEY:
        params["key"] = PSI_KEY
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=60) as c:
        r = await c.get(PSI_URL, params=params)
        r.raise_for_status()
        data = r.json()
    lh = data.get("lighthouseResult", {})
    audits = lh.get("audits", {})
    lcp_ms = audits.get("largest-contentful-paint", {}).get("numericValue")
    perf = lh.get("categories", {}).get("performance", {}).get("score")
    return {
        "lcp": round(lcp_ms / 1000, 1) if lcp_ms else None,
        "perf": round(perf * 100) if perf is not None else None,
    }


async def measure_speed(url: str) -> dict:
    """
    Returns real measured numbers when PSI succeeds, else {} so the
    caller falls back to the httpx estimate. Never raises.
    """
    if not url:
        return {}
    if not url.startswith("http"):
        url = "https://" + url
    if not PSI_KEY:
        return {}  # no key configured — caller uses estimate
    try:
        mobile, desktop = await asyncio.gather(
            _run(url, "mobile"),
            _run(url, "desktop"),
            return_exceptions=True,
        )
        out = {}
        if isinstance(mobile, dict):
            out["psi_mobile_lcp"] = mobile.get("lcp")
            out["psi_mobile_perf"] = mobile.get("perf")
        if isinstance(desktop, dict):
            out["psi_desktop_lcp"] = desktop.get("lcp")
            out["psi_desktop_perf"] = desktop.get("perf")
        return {k: v for k, v in out.items() if v is not None}
    except Exception:
        return {}

That's the whole file. The one comment with an em dash is inside Python code (a comment), so it has zero effect on anything a prospect sees, but if you'd rather keep it clean I can strip it.

What happened: the file has em dashes (and emoji) in it, saved in UTF-8. But Python 3.14 on Windows defaulted to reading it as cp1252 (the old Windows encoding), which can't decode byte 0x8d — that's a fragment of a UTF-8 em dash. What broke it: Set-Content -Encoding UTF8 on Windows PowerShell 5.1 writes a BOM (byte order mark, U+FEFF) at the very start of the file. Python sees that invisible character before the """ and chokes. So the em-dash replace worked, but the write added a poison byte at position zero.

$content = $content -replace [char]0xFEFF, ''
[System.IO.File]::WriteAllText("$PWD\db\harvester.py", $content, (New-Object System.Text.UTF8Encoding $false))

The New-Object System.Text.UTF8Encoding $false is the key bit — the $false means "no BOM". That strips the existing BOM and writes clean UTF-8.
